title: The Bell Beneath Brackenmere
description: A bell rings beneath a storm-bound village. Follow the water, the old verses, and a missing bellkeeper before the flood arrives.
tagline: When the mountain answers, listen to the water.
theme: Brackenmere is a highland village of slate roofs, spring-fed canals, and old stonework. A storm has cut off the road on the eve of the Lantern Sounding. At 9:06, the tower bell rings although its rope has been severed. Bellkeeper Edda Moss is missing, and the flood channel is rising.

caseSubject.name: Edda Moss
caseSubject.description: Edda has been updating the old spring maps. Find her before the flood rises.
caseSubject.recoveredDescription: Edda is safe. Her spring maps helped trace the water's hidden route.

chapters.title: The Silent Bell Tower
chapters.subtitle: The bell rang from below the village.
chapters.intro: The storm has sealed Brackenmere's mountain road. The tower bell sounded once at 9:06, though the bell rope lies cut on the floor. Edda Moss, the village bellkeeper, has not come home. The flood channel will crest before dawn. You are here to help read the old water maps; first, find out what that impossible bell was trying to tell you.

evidence.title: The severed bell rope
evidence.detail: The hemp fibers are cleanly cut and still dry. There is no dust on the cut surface, so it happened recently. The rope could not have pulled the bell at 9:06.
evidence.note: Fresh cut; bell rope could not ring the tower bell.

evidence.title: The bellkeeper's ledger
evidence.detail: Edda's careful hand records one entry: “9:06 — one low note, fourteen seconds. Heard through the floor. No wind.” Beside it she has drawn a small wave beneath a bell.
evidence.note: At 9:06, one low note came through the floor.

document.heading: Bellkeeper's ledger
lines: Heard through the floor. No wind.
document.annotation: A small wave is drawn beneath a bell beside this entry.

evidence.title: A note beneath the map
evidence.detail: A damp corner of the village flood map has lifted. Under it, Edda wrote: “If it sounds again, check the stone where the tide forgets.” The graphite is smudged toward the old pumping quarter.
evidence.note: Edda points toward the old pumping quarter.

document.heading: Village flood map
lines: The old channel runs from the tower foundations toward the pumping quarter.
document.annotation: Note beneath the lifted corner: “If it sounds again, check the stone where the tide forgets.”

characters.name: Rian Holt
characters.bio: Practical and quick to notice a faulty valve. He has been working late at the pumping station.

questions.ask: What could make a bell sound without its rope?
questions.reply: A bell can answer a vibration. There are old overflow pipes beneath the tower, but I cannot tell what made that low note from here.
questions.followUp: Then the note may have come from the waterworks, not the tower?
questions.followReply: That's my best guess. But I'd want the pressure records before I called it a cause.

questions.ask: When did you last see Edda?
questions.reply: Just before the storm. She asked whether the lower bypass still opened. I told her it was chained until the water dropped.
questions.followUp: Did she say why she was asking?
questions.followReply: Only that the old spring needed listening to. I thought she meant the bell.

questions.ask: Can you help me read the flood map?
questions.reply: Yes. The newer channels are marked in blue. The old stone run is faint, but it joins the tower foundations to the pumping quarter.
questions.followUp: So the map's pale line is still part of the system?
questions.followReply: It should be. The town stopped maintaining it, but the water never signed that agreement.

characters.name: Jori Wren
characters.bio: Bright, observant, and worried about Edda. Jori knows the tower's old routines.

questions.ask: Where were you when the bell rang?
questions.reply: On the lower stair. I heard the note through the stone first. The bell above me barely moved.
questions.followUp: Did anyone else hear it?
questions.followReply: The whole square did. Everyone looked up. I was the only one looking down.

questions.ask: What was Edda doing before she disappeared?
questions.reply: She took her brass lantern and the old map. She said she needed to check a place that “only exists when the water is low.”
questions.followUp: Did she say where that was?
questions.followReply: No. But she tapped the map right where the old spring is drawn.

questions.ask: Could the cut rope be an accident?
questions.reply: Not the way it was cut. The fibers are too clean for a tear. I don't know who used a blade or when.
questions.followUp: Do you know who cut it?
questions.followReply: No. The cut looks deliberate, but I don't know who made it or when.

puzzle.title: Read the signal
puzzle.prompt: The bell sounded at 9:06 despite its severed rope. Where should you investigate next?

options.label: Search the tower for whoever pulled the rope.
Follow Edda's note toward the old pumping quarter.
Conclude that a supernatural presence sounded the bell.
Assume the bell sounded before the rope was cut.

puzzle.success: The rope cannot explain the low note. Edda's map points toward the old pumping quarter, where the next answer may lie.

hints: Start with what the ledger says about the sound.
The severed rope rules out an ordinary pull. What direction did Edda leave behind?
The map points toward the old pumping quarter. Follow that lead.
chapters.clue: Edda's note points toward the old pumping quarter. The cause of the low note is still unknown.

environment.layout: Bell centered above two work surfaces; the severed rope lies on the left floor, the map in the foreground, and Edda’s ledger on the right desk.
environment.lighting: Warm lantern light from both sides meets cold storm light through the rear arch.

objects.name: The severed bell rope
objects.appearance: Frayed, cleanly severed pale hemp coil on wet stone; free end points toward the bell frame.

objects.name: The bellkeeper's ledger
objects.appearance: Open dark leather ledger with cream pages, resting on the right wooden desk beside the lantern.

objects.name: A note beneath the map
objects.appearance: Weathered flood map spread on the foreground crate; a separate small note peeks beneath its lower edge.

chapters.title: The Old Pump House
chapters.subtitle: Water leaves a record even when people do not.
chapters.intro: The pumping quarter sits below the tower, where rainwater runs into the village's oldest channels. Rian's current gauges tell only part of the story; the stonework has older routes, and Edda's lantern is nowhere in the main room.

evidence.title: The pressure gauge
evidence.detail: The needle is pinned just above the safe mark. A thin crescent of fresh water sits inside the glass. The pressure rose sharply and fell again, as if a valve opened briefly upstream.
evidence.note: A brief pressure surge passed through the old line.

evidence.title: The valve chart
evidence.detail: A hand-drawn chart names four points: East Sluice, Orchard Stair, Aqueduct Bend, and Springworks. An arrow traces a service route downhill. The Springworks gate is circled in Edda's blue pencil.
evidence.note: Edda marked a route from East Sluice to Springworks.

document.heading: Valve route chart
lines: The marked route runs downhill through all four points.
document.annotation: Edda circled the Springworks gate in blue pencil.

evidence.title: A damp lantern wick
evidence.detail: A brass lantern rests behind a drain grate. Its wick is damp but not burned down. A strand of blue wool clings to the hinge; it matches Edda's coat in her case portrait.
evidence.note: Edda's lantern was here recently; she continued below.

evidence.title: The ferry key ledger
evidence.detail: The key book shows that the lower sluice key was signed out to Marit Pell at 8:40, then returned at 8:53. The return line is written in a different ink from the issue line.
evidence.note: The lower sluice key's return entry may not be genuine.

document.heading: Ferry key ledger
document.annotation: The return line was written in a different ink.

characters.name: Marit Pell
characters.bio: A steady ferry warden who keeps the lower-channel keys and knows the village's crossings.

questions.ask: Did you use the lower sluice key?
questions.reply: I signed it out to Rian. He said the east channel was backing up. I returned the key before nine, but I can't swear who wrote the return line.
questions.followUp: Why lend it if the gate was chained?
questions.followReply: Because a chain is not the same thing as a safe channel. I wanted someone who knew the valves to check it.

questions.ask: Did you see Edda near the ferry?
questions.reply: Not at the landing. I saw her lantern light under the old stone arch, on the pump-house side.
questions.followUp: Could she have reached the lower passage from there?
questions.followReply: At low water, yes. There's a service stair the maps stopped showing years ago.

questions.ask: Does the key ledger look right to you?
questions.reply: The return time is too neat. I use a hooked seven; this one is straight. Someone copied my signature from the issue line.
questions.followUp: Who had reason to copy it?
questions.followReply: Rian had the key. That doesn't tell us why he wanted the record to look clean.

characters.name: Rian Holt
characters.bio: He understands the channels, but he is withholding something about the valves.

questions.ask: What caused the pressure to jump?
questions.reply: A gate opening and closing would do it. So would water hitting a narrowed pipe. I need the route chart to know which is more likely.
questions.followUp: Could the same surge ring the tower bell?
questions.followReply: If the pipe meets the tower footing, yes. The stone could turn pressure into a low note.

questions.ask: What does Edda's route chart mean?
questions.reply: Those four points make a maintenance path. East Sluice feeds the orchard stair, then the aqueduct bend, then the springworks.
questions.followUp: Why circle the final gate?
questions.followReply: It's the one that can isolate the old spring without flooding the village.

questions.ask: Why was your name on the key?
questions.reply: I borrowed it to open a side-channel for the upper hamlet. Their well ran dry. I meant to return before the storm rose.
questions.followUp: Why hide that from Marit?
questions.followReply: I thought I could put everything back before anyone noticed. Then the gate jammed, and Edda went looking for the pressure drop.

puzzle.title: Trace Edda's route
puzzle.prompt: Reconstruct Edda's marked service route from East Sluice to Springworks. Select the checkpoints in the order she would pass them.
puzzle.success: The marked service route leads from East Sluice through Orchard Stair and Aqueduct Bend to Springworks. Edda's lantern continued toward the lower works. The pressure surge and the ledger's different ink remain leads to investigate.

hints: Trace Edda's route checkpoints on the chart. The key ledger is a separate lead; its different ink does not prove what happened.
Begin at East Sluice. The water and the service path both move downhill. Tap a selected valve again to remove it from your route.
East Sluice → Orchard Stair → Aqueduct Bend → Springworks Gate.
chapters.clue: The side-channel and the marked service path converge at the Springworks.

environment.layout: The chart is fixed to the left wall, the gauge sits high on a right pipe, Edda’s lantern is behind the central floor grate, and the key ledger lies on the right bench.
environment.lighting: Warm pipe-house lanterns against cool rainy light through the open door.

objects.name: The pressure gauge
objects.appearance: Round cream-faced pressure gauge in a tarnished brass rim, bolted to the upper right pipe.

objects.name: The valve chart
objects.appearance: Aging parchment valve-route diagram pinned flat to the left timber board.

objects.name: A damp lantern wick
objects.appearance: Small lit brass lantern beneath the central drain grate; damp wick and blue wool at its hinge.

objects.name: The ferry key ledger
objects.appearance: Open key ledger with one black iron key resting diagonally across its pages on the right workbench.

chapters.title: The Listening Aqueduct
chapters.subtitle: The old verse describes a sound, not a spirit.
chapters.intro: The aqueduct is a narrow stone gallery over the gorge. Here, the village's oldest tale says the Echo Keeper answers when someone disturbs the spring. Sella Fen has spent years collecting the verses. The current marks and the pressure chart may tell whether the story is warning, memory, or both.

evidence.title: The water marks
evidence.detail: Three mineral lines mark the recent water heights. The newest line stops below the bell pipe. The pipe itself is dry at the upper joint, but dark water beads at its lower bend.
evidence.note: The bell pipe carries water only at its lower bend.

evidence.title: The pipe diagram
evidence.detail: A maintenance drawing shows a narrow iron pipe running beneath the tower footing. At the aqueduct bend, the pipe narrows before opening into a stone resonator chamber.
evidence.note: A narrow pipe meets a hollow stone chamber beneath the tower.

evidence.title: The Echo Keeper verse
evidence.detail: The carved verse reads: “When spring is bound and narrow made, the quiet stone will sing. Unbind the path beneath the roots, and let the flood go wing.” The last line is worn, but the word “roots” is clear.
evidence.note: The folklore describes a bound spring, a narrow passage, and a release.

evidence.title: A tuning fork on stone
evidence.detail: A small tuning fork lies beside the resonator. When touched to the stone, its note lasts several seconds. A fresh scrape on the chamber lip shows something heavy moved here recently.
evidence.note: The hollow stone sustains a vibration; something was moved recently.

characters.name: Sella Fen
characters.bio: A patient local historian who treats old stories as records of what people learned to survive.

questions.ask: Who is the Echo Keeper?
questions.reply: In the oldest version, no one. It is the sound the spring makes when its way is pinched. Later tellers gave the sound a name so children would remember to clear the winter channel.
questions.followUp: So the story may preserve an instruction?
questions.followReply: A good folktale often carries a practical truth farther than a maintenance notice.

questions.ask: What does “beneath the roots” mean here?
questions.reply: There is an old spring garden above the works. Its roots grew over a service hatch. The verse is pointing to a place, not asking us to dig blindly.
questions.followUp: Does the garden connect to the aqueduct?
questions.followReply: A stone drain runs from its well to this gallery. The map calls it a dead end, but the verse says otherwise.

questions.ask: Has the bell ever sounded like this before?
questions.reply: Once, during the drought of '68. The spring was throttled to keep water for the manor. The bell rang until the workers opened the bypass.
questions.followUp: Was anyone in danger then?
questions.followReply: The lower garden flooded ankle-deep. No one was trapped. The story remembers the sound because it warned them in time.

characters.name: Rian Holt
characters.bio: The pressure chart has brought him back to the old channel he hoped to keep quiet.

questions.ask: Could this pipe really ring the bell?
questions.reply: The pipe narrows, then opens into a hollow chamber. A sudden flow would pulse against it. The tower footing would carry that vibration like a sounding board.
questions.followUp: Would the note last fourteen seconds?
questions.followReply: With water still moving through the bend, yes. The chamber would keep the note alive after the first surge.

questions.ask: What did you divert to the upper hamlet?
questions.reply: A small share of the spring. Their well failed, and the council's repair was weeks away. I opened a side-channel without permission.
questions.followUp: Did you know it would change the bell pipe?
questions.followReply: I thought the bypass was sealed. I should have tested the whole line before opening anything.

questions.ask: Why did Edda go down to the springworks?
questions.reply: She heard the pressure drop and knew the old bypass might be caught. She went to free the counterweight. I should have gone with her.
questions.followUp: Do you think she's hurt?
questions.followReply: The lower alcove is above the flood line at this height. We need to reach her before it rises further.

puzzle.title: Explain the bell
puzzle.prompt: Which explanation best fits the evidence?

options.label: A pressure surge traveled through the narrow pipe and excited the hollow stone resonator, producing the sustained note.
Someone pulled the tower bell rope from inside the tower.
The storm wind alone made the bell sound.
The sound was caused by a supernatural presence.

puzzle.success: A pressure surge through the narrow pipe set the hollow stone resonator vibrating. The tower footing carried the sustained note. This explains the apparent bell sound without a pulled rope, but it does not explain who severed that rope or settle the other leads.

hints: Compare where the water is wet with where the pipe narrows.
The bell pipe meets a hollow chamber. The tuning fork shows how long the stone can hold a note.
A brief pressure surge through the narrow pipe could make the stone resonator sustain the low note.
chapters.clue: The “Echo Keeper” is the pressure resonance of the old spring system.

environment.layout: The verse relief and mineral lines share the left wall, while a pipe diagram is mounted above the right-hand resonator and a tuning fork rests on its stone ledge.
environment.lighting: Warm wall lantern near the relief; cold storm light across the river and right wall.

objects.name: The water marks
objects.appearance: Three pale mineral tide lines running across the lower left stone wall, newest line below the pipe.

objects.name: The pipe diagram
objects.appearance: Worn engineering drawing pinned on a dry upper-right board above the iron pipe.

objects.name: The Echo Keeper verse
objects.appearance: Relief-carved folklore panel set into the left masonry, with weathered verse detailing.

objects.name: A tuning fork on stone
objects.appearance: Small steel tuning fork placed on the dry resonator ledge beside a fresh scrape.

chapters.title: The Old Spring Garden
chapters.subtitle: The verse is also a map.
chapters.intro: Behind the aqueduct, bracken covers a terraced garden around the original spring. Four carved stones carry the rest of Sella's verse. Edda's lantern was seen below this level. The storm water is rising, so read the route carefully before opening anything.

evidence.title: The four verse stones
evidence.detail: The stones read: “Face the first light”; “where the reed roots drink”; “below the third arch”; “the spring door waits.” Their lichen is rubbed away on the eastern edges, as if someone traced a route with a lantern.
evidence.note: The verse gives four ordered landmarks, oriented toward the east.

evidence.title: The spring-garden map
evidence.detail: A survey map puts the east-facing stone at the garden entrance. A reed bed borders the old well. Three arches cross the lower terrace; a narrow stair descends beneath the third.
evidence.note: The map matches all four landmarks in the verse.

evidence.title: The lantern trail
evidence.detail: Drops of lamp oil mark the garden's lower stair. The trail goes beneath the third arch and stops at a stone panel. One edge has been forced inward from the other side.
evidence.note: Edda reached a stone door beneath the third arch.

evidence.title: The counterweight mark
evidence.detail: A chalk arrow points down beside the panel. Under it: “Don't lift against the water. Release the weight after the bypass is open.” Edda's handwriting is hurried but legible.
evidence.note: Open the bypass first; release the counterweight only after the water drops.

characters.name: Jori Wren
characters.bio: Jori has followed Edda's lantern trail and recognizes the old service marks.

questions.ask: Can the stone panel be opened from here?
questions.reply: Not safely. The water presses against it. Edda taught me never to pull a gate before the channel has somewhere to drain.
questions.followUp: Did she teach you the order?
questions.followReply: Open the bypass, wait for the level to fall, then free the weight. She made me repeat it until I stopped rushing.

questions.ask: What does the chalk mark mean?
questions.reply: Down, not up. The counterweight is holding the panel against the current. If we lift it now, the water could slam the door shut.
questions.followUp: And after the bypass is open?
questions.followReply: The pressure will ease. Then the weight can lower the panel gently.

questions.ask: Did Edda know the passage was flooded?
questions.reply: She knew it would be wet, not that the side-channel was open. She took a line and a lamp. She was trying to reach the lower gate, not hide from us.
questions.followUp: Could she signal if she heard us?
questions.followReply: Tap the bell pipe twice. It carries sound down to the alcove.

characters.name: Sella Fen
characters.bio: She can translate the old verse into the landmarks on the survey map.

questions.ask: How do we read the verse stones?
questions.reply: Start where the first light enters: east. Follow the reeds to the well, count the arches, and descend at the third. The verse is a path written for people who knew the garden.
questions.followUp: Why hide a route in a song?
questions.followReply: So the children who learned the harvest song would also remember where the flood passage was.

questions.ask: What is behind the spring door?
questions.reply: The old works. It was built to let people reach the spring without crossing the flooded channel.
questions.followUp: Could Edda be there now?
questions.followReply: If she went to free the gate, the alcove is the safest place to wait.

questions.ask: Why does the verse mention roots?
questions.reply: The spring's roots, literal and remembered. The garden grew over the service stair. What looks like a dead end is the way down.
questions.followUp: The folklore keeps the maintenance route alive?
questions.followReply: Exactly. People tend to preserve a song longer than a stone sign.

puzzle.title: Follow the verse
puzzle.prompt: Read the stones and the garden survey, then trace four landmarks from the eastern entrance to the hidden door.

items.label: Face the first light at the east entrance
Follow the reed roots to the old well

puzzle.success: The verse leads from the east-facing stone, past the reeds and beneath the third arch. Edda's lantern trail ends at the spring door. You have found the way to her; opening the water-pressed panel is the next problem.

hints: Use the map to match the verse's named landmarks.
The first light tells you where to begin. The reeds and three arches give the next two steps.
East entrance → reed well → third arch → spring door.
chapters.clue: Edda is beyond the spring door; the bypass must drain before the counterweight moves.

environment.layout: Four verse stones stand on the middle terrace; the survey map is on the right bench, a lantern marks the left lower stair, and a chalk arrow is on the lower center service door.
environment.lighting: Moonlit blue terraces with small warm lantern pools on the stairs.

objects.name: The four verse stones
objects.appearance: Four distinct mossed verse stones with worn faces, standing together on the middle terrace.

objects.name: The spring-garden map
objects.appearance: Folded survey parchment lying flat on a dry right-hand stone bench.

objects.name: The lantern trail
objects.appearance: Small brass lantern on the lower-left stair with scattered droplets of lamp oil.

objects.name: The counterweight mark
objects.appearance: White chalk arrow drawn down the lower service door beneath the third arch.

chapters.title: The Springworks
chapters.subtitle: One safe sequence can open the way.
chapters.intro: The lower chamber is filling. Through the stone panel you hear two careful taps: Edda is alive and waiting in the service alcove. Rian admits that he diverted water to the drought-struck upper hamlet. The unauthorized side-channel changed the pressure and jammed the bypass. Restore the safe flow before the chamber rises another foot.

evidence.title: The gate diagram
evidence.detail: The diagram shows the bypass draining toward the east channel. The spring door is held by a counterweight. A red warning reads: “Never release weight under head pressure.”

readableDetail.heading: Gate and bypass · readable drawing key
readableDetail.warning: Never release weight under head pressure.

evidence.note: The bypass drains the chamber; the counterweight is safe only after the level falls.

evidence.title: The rising waterline
evidence.detail: The newest water mark is two hand-widths above the safe line. The bypass wheel is stuck but not locked. The side-channel valve is open just enough to keep pressure in the old bell pipe.
evidence.note: The side channel is open; pressure still feeds the resonant pipe.

evidence.title: Edda's tool roll
evidence.detail: A wrench, a length of dry rope, and Edda's brass whistle lie on the ledge. The wrench fits the bypass wheel. A note on the roll says, “Two turns, then listen.”
evidence.note: Edda prepared to open the bypass and signal from the alcove.

evidence.title: The upper-hamlet tally
evidence.detail: A folded page lists the hamlet's dry wells and the number of households relying on the spring. Rian has added: “Temporary line, until the council repairs their catchment.” His motive was to help, but the diversion was unsafe and hidden.

readableDetail.heading: Upper hamlet water tally · readable transcription
labels: Dry wells are recorded for the upper hamlet.
The page tallies households relying on the spring.
Rian's note: “Temporary line, until the council repairs their catchment.”
readableDetail.warning: No household figures are clear enough here to transcribe reliably.

evidence.note: Rian's hidden diversion was meant to help the upper hamlet.

characters.name: Rian Holt
characters.bio: He has admitted opening the side-channel and is ready to help repair the system.

questions.ask: Why did you open the side-channel?
questions.reply: The upper hamlet's wells ran dry. I thought I could spare them water without hurting Brackenmere. I was wrong to do it alone, and wrong to hide the key record.
questions.followUp: Did you know Edda was in the lower passage?
questions.followReply: No. When the pressure dropped, she went to free the bypass. I should have told the others and gone with her.

questions.ask: What's the safest way to reach Edda?
questions.reply: Open the bypass and let the chamber drain. Then release the counterweight. The door will settle instead of surging against the water.
questions.followUp: Can we restore the shared flow after she's safe?
questions.followReply: Yes. We can close the side-channel after the gate is clear, then inspect the catchment together.

questions.ask: Was the bell your warning?
questions.reply: No. It was the pipe. I heard it too, but I was ashamed to say what I'd changed.
questions.followUp: The sound brought us here anyway.
questions.followReply: Edda used that sound to find the pressure fault. She understood the old system better than I did.

characters.name: Marit Pell
characters.bio: Marit is ready to coordinate the village once Edda is out.

questions.ask: Can the alcove hold until the water drops?
questions.reply: For a few minutes, yes. I can hear Edda tapping. We need to keep the door level when it opens.
questions.followUp: What should happen after she is safe?
questions.followReply: Close the side-channel and share the water records. Nobody should have to risk a flood to get a neighbor a drink.

questions.ask: How will Edda know we're opening the bypass?
questions.reply: Two taps on the pipe. Then give her a moment to move clear of the door.
questions.followUp: And if she doesn't answer?
questions.followReply: We stop. We don't force a gate with someone on the other side.

questions.ask: What happens to the upper hamlet now?
questions.reply: They still need water. We can bring their needs to the council and make a shared schedule that doesn't put either village at risk.
questions.followUp: Rian should have asked first.
questions.followReply: Yes. And the council should have listened before a well ran dry. We can hold both truths at once.

puzzle.title: Open the spring door safely
puzzle.prompt: Use Edda's note and the gate diagram to propose a safe rescue. The door lowers when its counterweight is released after pressure falls.

items.label: Verify the water is below the safe line
items.caption: Never release weight under head pressure

items.label: Signal and listen for Edda's answer
items.caption: Two turns, then listen

items.label: Release the counterweight
items.caption: The spring door lowers when safe

items.label: Close the side-channel after Edda is clear
items.caption: Stop the unauthorized diversion

puzzle.success: The bypass drains the chamber. The water falls below the safe line. Edda answers the signal; the counterweight releases under safe pressure and the spring door lowers. Once she is clear, the side-channel is closed. Edda is safe.

hints: The gate diagram warns against releasing the weight under head pressure.
Open the bypass two turns, then check the safe line and listen for Edda before moving the weight.
Bypass → verify safe water level → signal and listen → release counterweight → close side-channel after Edda is clear.
chapters.clue: Edda is safe. The pressure and stone explain the sound, while the severed rope and key entry remain unresolved.

endings.label: Bring the records to the council
endings.text: You share the pressure chart, the key record, and the upper-hamlet tally. Rian accepts responsibility. The council creates a joint catchment repair and a public water schedule. Sella adds the true story of the Echo Keeper to the Lantern Sounding: a warning made by water, remembered by people.

endings.label: Help the villages make a water pact
endings.text: You ask Rian and Marit to sit with the upper hamlet before the council meeting. They draft an emergency water pact and a repair plan together, then publish the records so no one has to guess what happened. At the next Lantern Sounding, Edda rings the bell by hand, and the villages answer from the hillside.

environment.layout: The floodgate and counterweight dominate the left chamber; a dry diagram rests on the left ledge, Edda’s tools are centered, and the tally and waterline sit on the right wall.
environment.lighting: Warm practical lanterns on stone ledges against cool water and tunnel light.

objects.name: The gate diagram
objects.appearance: Gate-and-bypass engineering diagram held by a metal clip on the dry left ledge.

objects.name: The rising waterline
objects.appearance: Fresh wet line above an older safe mark on the right stone beside the side valve.

objects.name: Edda's tool roll
objects.appearance: Open brown canvas tool roll carrying a wrench, coil of rope, brass whistle, and small note.

objects.name: The upper-hamlet tally
objects.appearance: Folded household water tally pinned to a dry upper-right board.

lines.speaker: Edda Moss
lines.text: I can. I thought the water would reach the alcove before anyone found the bypass.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: We followed your map. And the bell.

lines.speaker: Edda Moss
lines.text: Then the old warning still works. The stone carries the sound when water is driven through that narrow passage. I hoped someone would understand it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The pressure gauge in the pump house showed a surge.

lines.speaker: Edda Moss
lines.text: That would fit. The diversion sent water through the old line, and the resonator carried the vibration up toward the tower.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What about the lower sluice key? The return entry looks different.

lines.speaker: Edda Moss
lines.text: The ledger tells you when someone wrote that the key was returned. It doesn't tell you everything that happened while it was away. I wouldn't accuse anyone from the ink alone.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Why did Rian divert the water?

lines.speaker: Edda Moss
lines.text: The upper hamlet's wells were running dry. He was trying to help them, but he used a route that wasn't safe under these conditions.

lines.speaker: Edda Moss
lines.text: I don't know who cut it. The sound we heard didn't need the rope, but that doesn't explain why it was severed.

openingIntroduction.title: A Worrying Absence
text: Edda Moss, Brackenmere's bellkeeper, has not returned home.
During the storm, the tower bell sounded once at 9:06, even though its rope lies severed on the floor.
The mountain road is closed, the floodwater is rising, and Edda's old maps may be the only way to understand what happened.
Begin at the bell tower. Examine what she left behind.
